vote/paths: Sample a chain of thought at a temperature above zero, and every run takes a different path. Ask for seventeen times twenty four, five times.
vote/answers: Most paths reach four hundred and eight, by different routes. One slips to three hundred and ninety eight, another to four hundred and eighteen.
vote/vote: Self-consistency ignores the paths and counts the final answers. Four hundred and eight has three votes of five, so it wins.
vote/greedy: This needs real sampling. As the temperature goes to zero, greedy decoding writes the same path every time, and five copies of one answer add nothing.
vote/compare: And the vote needs answers that can be compared: a number, a letter, yes or no. Five stories never match word for word, so there is nothing to count.
try/p1: Try one. Asked for fifteen percent of eighty, a model samples seven chains of thought. Their final answers are fifteen, twelve, twelve, eight, twelve, fifteen and twelve. What does self-consistency return?
try/a1: Count each answer: twelve four times, fifteen twice, and eight once. Twelve has the most votes, four of seven, so twelve is returned.
try/not: Not the first path's fifteen: that is one path. And not the average, about twelve point two nine: a number no path reached.
try/p2: Now each of five replies to a multiple-choice question ends in a letter, A to D. Can the vote pick a better reply than one sample?
try/a2: Yes. Different paths often end on the same letter, so letters can be counted. Here three of the five end in B, so B wins.
